raw.answer: A clinic's responsible doctor was fined NT$50,000 after the clinic collected the full fee for a six-session laser hair removal course in one payment without getting the local health authority to approve that way of charging. The doctor argued the fee rules were too vague and limited professional and contract freedom too much. The Constitutional Court held that the rules are clear enough and proportionate, and rejected the challenge to the court judgment.
raw.held: The Medical Care Act provisions on fee standards and charging items (Articles 21 and 22(2)) are not unconstitutionally vague. These provisions and the related enforcement rule (Article 11(3)) do not violate the proportionality principle, the freedom to practice a profession, or freedom of contract. The doctor's petition against the court judgment was dismissed.

points.text: Read together, the two articles aim to stop clinics from inventing charges or overcharging, and the clinics they regulate can understand and foresee what they require.

'Fee standards' and 'charging items' include a course of repeated identical treatment, with its number of sessions and total cost, which must be backed by medical practice and approved by the local authority. Clinics already apply for pre-approval of such courses.
The rules limit clinics' freedom to practice and freedom to contract to some degree, but that is allowed if the aim is a proper public interest and the means reasonably relate to it.
Patients and clinics have very unequal medical knowledge, and fees affect people's ability to afford care and their health, so advance approval of fee amounts and items serves a proper purpose.
Review by local authorities and committees with medical professionals reasonably helps cut the information gap and prevent unreasonable fees, while also respecting clinics' legitimate interests.
Because the rules are constitutional and the judgment, including its use of the ministry's letters, showed no basic misunderstanding of rights, the petition against the judgment was dismissed.

who: Private clinics and their responsible doctors
Patients seeking medical or cosmetic treatment

raw.answer: A woman who passed the written part of the 2018 fire-police exam was later removed from training because a re-measurement showed she was 158.9 cm, below the 160 cm minimum for women. Taiwan's Constitutional Court held that applying the height minimum (165 cm for men, 160 cm for women) to the fire-police category breaches the constitutional guarantee of equality. It held that the separate rule allowing re-examination 'when necessary' is clear enough, and it sent her case back to the Supreme Administrative Court.
raw.held: The women's height standard, as applied to fire-police exam candidates, is inconsistent with the constitutional equality guarantee and loses effect at the latest one year after the ruling. The 'when necessary' re-examination rule is not unconstitutionally vague. The Supreme Administrative Court judgment is unconstitutional, set aside, and sent back.

points.text: The court applied intermediate scrutiny because the rule distinguishes by sex, a trait people are born with and can hardly change. The aim must be an important public interest and the means must be substantially related to it.

The height rule has an unequal effect: it excludes about 10% of men but about 55% of women, a statistically significant and long-stable gap, so it disadvantages women in the right to take public service exams.
The goal of making sure firefighters can carry out duties safely and effectively is an important public interest and is legitimate.

The means are not substantially related to that goal. The rule deepens the gender imbalance (88% men, 12% women), equipment can be adapted, stretcher-carrying problems arise with any height mismatch, and the agency admitted having no scientific evidence that people under 160 cm are dangerous in the job. Fire work is also varied, and shorter staff have advantages in some settings.

The authorities relied only on experience and tacit knowledge without sufficient evidence, so the rule fails equal protection. Any revision should keep the proportions of women and men excluded from being too far apart.

The 're-examination when necessary' rule is clear enough: it is understandable, foreseeable for those covered, and reviewable by courts. A re-check is allowed only when objective circumstances show a clear mismatch with the earlier exam.

Because the height rule is unconstitutional, the judgment applying it is also unconstitutional. The Supreme Administrative Court must decide her case in line with this ruling, without waiting for the one-year deadline.

raw.answer: After Taiwan's legislature passed amendments to the Legislative Yuan Functions and Powers Act and added a criminal offence (Criminal Code Article 141-1, contempt of the legislature), lawmakers, the Executive Yuan, the President and the Control Yuan challenged them. The Constitutional Court held that the lawmaking process was flawed but not fatally so. It struck down many provisions as exceeding the legislature's powers, and upheld others only on conditions it set out.
raw.held: The Act and Article 141-1 were not invalid because of the lawmaking process. Many provisions were struck down from the date of the judgment, including the President's state-of-the-nation report duties, parts of the questioning rules, parts of the nomination-consent and investigation rules, and the hearing penalties. Criminal Code Article 141-1 was also struck down. Other provisions were upheld only on the conditions the court set.

points.text: The lawmaking process was flawed, with very limited real debate and one-sided show-of-hands votes. But the draft bills had been reviewed in committee, public hearings were held, and the show-of-hands votes were not fully anonymous. So the process did not completely abandon the openness and discussion principles. Voters can hold lawmakers to account for it.

The President is not constitutionally required to give a report to the legislature, and the legislature may not set its content, question the President, or demand answers. Provisions imposing such duties exceed the legislature's powers and violate separation of powers.

Executive Yuan heads must answer legislators' questions, but this is a political responsibility, not a legal duty. The legislature may not impose penalties or fines, require its chair's consent to refuse, demand documents, send officials for impeachment or discipline, or make false statements a crime. Heads may decline to answer for good reasons such as state secrets, third-party rights or executive privilege.

Nominees' cooperation with the confirmation review is a burden they take on voluntarily, not a legal duty. The legislature's power is to consent or refuse, so it cannot impose duties or penalties on nominees beyond that.

The court made the legislature's investigative powers subject to conditions. Investigations must be tied to the legislature's constitutional powers, and the legislature may not investigate cases pending in court. Provisions such as the investigation special groups were struck down.

At hearings, people invited may be accompanied by a lawyer or other helper without the chair's consent. Government officials and members of the public may refuse for proper reasons, and fines for refusing were struck down as beyond the legislature's powers.

who: Nominees and people called to testify

raw.answer: A person convicted of making drug offences had about NT$92.87 million in cash confiscated because courts found it came from other illegal acts, beyond the drug crime itself. He challenged the confiscation rule (Article 19, paragraph 3 of the Narcotics Hazard Prevention Act) and the Criminal Code rule applying the law at the time of judgment as unconstitutional. The Constitutional Court held both rules constitutional, with conditions on how courts apply them, and rejected his petition.
raw.held: The extended confiscation rule is constitutional if "other illegal acts" means criminal acts, prosecutors prove the source, and courts find it highly probable the property came from other illegal acts, without relying only on the defendant's failure to show a lawful source. The Criminal Code rule, as it applies to this provision, is also constitutional, and the petition was dismissed.

points.text: Extended confiscation is not a punishment. Its aim is to strip illegal gains and restore a lawful property order, and it is not based on blame for past guilty conduct, so the principles on legality of crimes and punishments, culpability and presumption of innocence are not engaged.

It reaches only gains from other illegal acts, not the person's own lawful property, and it cannot be converted into detention or labor if it cannot be collected, which also shows it is not a penalty.
The rule is clear enough: "other illegal acts" means criminal acts, drawing on the Criminal Code's definition and the legislative reasons, and which specific crime it was is a question of evidence.

It meets the proportionality test and the property right: it serves an important public interest, there is no equally effective milder alternative, and it applies only to serious drug offences, with no double confiscation and a hardship adjustment available.

It respects fair trial if the prosecutor bears the burden of proof and the court finds it highly probable that the property came from other illegal acts. The court cannot rely solely on the defendant's inability to prove a lawful source, and the defendant must be able to respond and present evidence.

The Criminal Code rule is not a true retroactive law, because the illegal property order continues after the law took effect, and there is no protectable reliance interest in keeping such gains, so it does not breach non-retroactivity or reliance protection.

who: People convicted of serious drug offences

raw.answer: Many people challenged Taiwan's criminal law on public insult (Criminal Code Article 309, paragraph 1), arguing it violates free speech and is too vague. The Constitutional Court held the law is allowed only if it is read narrowly, so that it punishes serious, intentional insults that a person cannot reasonably be expected to tolerate and where reputation should outweigh free speech. It also found the term 'insult' clear enough, and sent four applicants' criminal convictions back to the lower courts for reconsideration.
raw.held: The public insult provision is not unconstitutional within the narrowed scope the court set out, and the term 'insult' is not unconstitutionally vague. The judgments against applicants 9, 10, 11 and 12 were found unconstitutional, set aside and sent back to the lower courts.

points.text: Insulting speech is not automatically worthless. It can carry political, literary, artistic, academic or public-debate value, and because a criminal record and possible detention burden speech, courts must weigh it against reputation.
The law's legitimate purpose is protecting social reputation and the equal standing and dignity of a person (reputation-personality). Hurt feelings alone are not protected by this criminal provision.

Read literally, the offence could sweep too widely, catching swear words, personal speech habits and criticism that serves public debate. So it is limited to intentional, context-based insults beyond what people can reasonably tolerate, after weighing the speech's value.

Criminal punishment is consistent with the last-resort principle for serious insults, such as targeting disadvantaged groups. Detention should be reserved for severe cases, such as online insults with lasting or spreading harm.

'Insult' is a value-laden concept that courts can interpret using ordinary methods, and ordinary people can understand it as demeaning someone's reputation. So it does not breach the clarity principle.

The four judgments failed to weigh properly whether the words truly harmed reputation or dignity beyond tolerable limits, or the speech's value, such as public-affairs debate or the victim being a self-media operator, so they were sent back.

who: Applicants 9 to 12 whose cases were sent back
Courts and prosecutors applying the law
People who say harsh things about others, online or in person

raw.answer: Taiwan's Constitutional Court reviewed Article 140 of the Criminal Code, which punishes insulting a public official while they lawfully perform their duties, and insulting the official duties themselves in public. It held that the offense of insulting an official is constitutional only in a narrow range, and that the offense of insulting official duties violates freedom of speech and loses effect from the date of the judgment. It also overturned a High Court judgment that had applied the invalid part.
raw.held: The insulting-an-official offense is valid only when the on-the-spot insult is made with the aim of obstructing official business and is enough to affect the official's performance of duty. The insulting-official-duties offense is unconstitutional and ceases to have effect from the judgment date. The High Court judgment for petitioners four and five is overturned and sent back, and part of petitioner one's request is not accepted.

points.text: Speech criticizing government power and officials gets high constitutional protection, and the state should tolerate harsh or emotional protest. The court therefore reviewed the insulting-duties offense strictly and the insulting-official offense at a medium level.

Protecting an official's personal reputation and protecting the dignity of public office are not valid purposes. The dignity of office is an outdated idea that conflicts with free speech and democracy. Only protecting the performance of official duties is a legitimate purpose, and only where the insult can actually affect that performance.

The insulting-an-official offense is an offense of obstructing official business. It must therefore require an intent to obstruct, and courts cannot infer that intent from the insult alone. Ordinary complaints or emotional outbursts usually do not obstruct official work.

The insult must clearly be able to interfere with the official's direction, coordination and carrying out of duties. Officials may first warn the speaker to stop. If the person keeps going after a warning, intent and effect may be found, and no warning is needed for physical contact or sustained abuse by many people.

The insulting-official-duties offense punishes criticism of government action, which lies at the core of protected speech. It is hard to imagine such abstract cursing clearly and immediately obstructing official work, and punishing it even with fines violates the principle that criminal law is a last resort. So it loses effect.
Because the High Court judgment applied the invalid insulting-duties provision, it is also unconstitutional and is overturned and sent back.

who: People who insult or criticize officials performing their duties
Public officials carrying out their duties
Petitioners four and five, whose conviction was overturned
Petitioners two and three, who may seek an extraordinary appeal

raw.answer: A substitute teacher in New Taipei City held a valid teaching certificate. The school did not count her two earlier years of substitute teaching when setting her pay, and she challenged that rule as unconstitutional. The Constitutional Court held that the delegation to the Ministry of Education was valid. It also held that letting local governments decide whether to count the prior years breaches the constitutional division of powers, and that not counting them breaches equality.
raw.held: The Court held the 2000 Teachers' Act delegation clause consistent with the principle of clear delegation. It held the Ministry's letting local governments set the rules, and New Taipei's rules not counting prior years, unconstitutional under Article 108(1)(4) and Article 7. Those parts lose effect within 1 year, and the petitioner may seek a retrial within 30 days of service of the judgment. The remaining petitions were not accepted.

points.text: The clause authorizing the Ministry to set substitute teachers' rights and duties is clear enough, because substitute teachers have a supplementary, special role that differs from full-time teachers.
Decision 707 covers non-full-time teachers too, so their pay must be set by law or by a regulation under a clear legal delegation.
Counting a certified substitute teacher's prior years is part of the education system and needs a nationally uniform rule set by the central government, not by each locality.
By leaving the question to local governments, the Ministry and New Taipei City effectively allowed local lawmaking on a central matter, which breaches Article 108(1)(4).
Not counting prior years treats certified substitutes differently from full-time teachers, though they do substantially the same work, so a medium level of review applies.
The cost-saving aim is of doubtful importance. The cost evidence was imprecise, and the means do not substantially serve the aim, so the unequal treatment breaches Article 7.

who: Certified substitute teachers in public schools below university level

raw.answer: People sentenced to life imprisonment who got parole, then had it revoked, were required to serve a fixed 20 or 25 more years. The Constitutional Court held that this fixed term is disproportionate and violates the constitutional protection of personal liberty, so it must be replaced by rules that vary with the circumstances.
raw.held: The fixed 20- or 25-year remaining term in Criminal Code Article 79-1(5) loses effect within 2 years of the ruling at the latest. If no new law is passed by then, authorities must handle each case proportionately instead. Certain petitioners' final rulings were quashed and sent back to the Supreme Court, and the transitional-application rules (Articles 7-1(2) and 7-2(2)) were held not to breach non-retroactivity or reliance protection.

points.text: Revoking parole and re-imprisoning someone restricts personal liberty, so serving the remaining sentence must meet the proportionality principle, including for life sentences.
The purpose of the rules (rehabilitation, preventing reoffending, protecting society) is legitimate.

A fixed term is not necessary: it ignores whether revocation was for a new crime or for breaking supervision rules, the seriousness of the new offence, and the parolee's efforts to reintegrate. This denies any reassessment and may impose more punishment than needed.
The ruling suggests, as an example, remaining terms of 5, 10, 15, 20 or 25 years depending on the sentence for the new offence or the type of violation.
Other prisoners serving such terms get the chance to have them reset, and time already served stays valid, with no compensation claims for it.
The transitional rules apply the law in force when the cause of revocation occurred, so they do not apply the law retroactively.

who: Life-sentence prisoners whose parole was revoked
The 35 petitioners and the Supreme Court
Prosecutors and courts handling sentence enforcement
Legislators who must amend the law

raw.answer: 37 people sentenced to death asked Taiwan's Constitutional Court to review whether the death penalty provisions for intentional killing offences, and the procedures used in death penalty cases, are constitutional. The court held that the death penalty for these offences is not unconstitutional, but only in the most serious cases and with the strictest procedural safeguards. It struck down a 1999 law making death the only penalty, and it required extra protections such as a lawyer present at questioning, a lawyer and oral hearing at the third trial level, and unanimous judges.
raw.held: The death penalty as the maximum sentence for these killing offences is allowed only where the crime is among the most serious and the process meets the strictest due process; the 1999 mandatory-death version of Article 348(1) is unconstitutional. The court also ordered new procedural safeguards, barred death sentences or executions for certain defendants with mental impairments, and allowed the applicants to seek case-specific relief; the requests for interim measures were rejected.

points.text: Life is the most important constitutional right but not absolute, so the death penalty is reviewed under a strict standard, as are its procedures.

The purpose of just retribution and deterrence is legitimate. Because death is irreversible, it may be used only for the most serious killings, meaning direct, general or alternative intent and a completed killing, with especially grave circumstances.
The 1999 version of Article 348(1) made death the only penalty regardless of how serious the case was, which is too harsh and violates the principle of culpability.
To avoid wrongful convictions, suspects need a lawyer present during questioning, and the third trial level needs mandatory defence counsel and an oral hearing before a death sentence.
A death sentence must be decided unanimously by the panel of judges, to ensure no reasonable doubt about the aggravating factors.

Defendants whose ability to tell right from wrong was markedly reduced at the time of the offence, or whose ability to defend themselves at trial is clearly insufficient, may not be sentenced to death. Those who lack capacity to understand the sentence may not be executed.

who: People facing death penalty charges for intentional killing
People with mental impairments or intellectual disabilities

raw.answer: A person posted comments on Facebook pages criticizing a local businessman, and was convicted of aggravated defamation (the public-insult charge was folded into it). The Constitutional Court found that the Penghu court's final judgment violated constitutional free speech protection, struck it down, and sent the case back to be decided again.
raw.held: The effect of the earlier Judgment No. 3 (its first and second items) also covers the challenge to the public-insult provision (Criminal Code Art. 309, para. 1) in this case. The Penghu District Court's judgment is unconstitutional, set aside, and sent back to that court.

points.text: The court accepted the case and heard the challenge to the public-insult provision together with 33 other cases that challenged the same provision.
Because the challenge to the provision was heard together with those cases, the earlier Judgment No. 3 (first and second items) applies to this case too.
The final judgment treated the comments as one act that met both the public-insult and the aggravated-defamation charges, so the court reviewed how both provisions were applied.

A public-insult conviction requires looking at the context of the speech, whether it went beyond what people can reasonably tolerate, and weighing the harm to reputation against the speech's possible value. The lower court did none of this, so its approach conflicts with free speech protection.

For defamation about matters of public interest, the court must consider whether the speaker made a reasonable effort to verify the claims and weigh reputation against free speech in the circumstances.

The lower court gave identical reasons for the defamation conviction and did not work out whether the speech concerned public interest, whether the truth defense applied, or how to balance the interests, so that part also violates free speech protection.
For these reasons the final judgment was held unconstitutional, set aside, and sent back to the Penghu District Court.

who: Criminal courts hearing insult and defamation cases

raw.answer: The case concerned a Taiwan tax rule that treats property a person gave to a spouse within 2 years before death as part of the estate for estate tax. Two petitioners challenged it: a court reviewing a case where the sole heir owed about NT$57 million in tax, and a spouse who was denied a deduction. The Constitutional Court held the rule unconstitutional in two respects and gave the legislature 2 years to fix it.
raw.held: The rule violates equal protection because it does not clearly say how the spouse and the other heirs share the tax, so other heirs can end up paying tax on the spouse's gain. It also violates equal protection by giving the spouse no deduction like the surplus-property-difference deduction in Article 17-1, and it infringes property rights where heirs' inheritance is severely reduced. The legislature must revise within 2 years, and the Taipei High Administrative Court judgment and the Supreme Administrative Court ruling are quashed and sent back.

points.text: Estate tax should follow each person's actual ability to pay, and any departure from that needs a legitimate public purpose with a reasonable link to it.
The rule aims to stop people avoiding estate tax by giving away property before death, which is a legitimate goal of tax fairness.
Taxing other heirs on the spouse's gain, with no rule on how the burden is shared, does not match their ability to pay and has no reasonable link to the goal, so it breaches equal protection.
With no cap or sharing rule, the tax can severely reduce or wipe out an heir's inheritance, which infringes property rights. The Ministry's limit of enforcement to the estate does not change this.

Gifted property is treated as estate property for tax, yet it gets no deduction for the spouse's economic contribution like other estate property. That difference is unrelated to the goal of closing tax gaps, so it breaches equal protection.

Until the law is amended, the tax on the deemed estate may be charged only to the spouse if the spouse is a taxpayer, or may not be charged to the heirs or collected from the estate if the spouse is not. Gifted property is also to be counted as existing property when working out the spouse's deduction.

who: Surviving spouses who received gifts within 2 years before death
